derivs.title: Minimizer of a quadratic
derivs.setup: Given f(x) = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx + c with H symmetric, derive the stationary point, the condition for it to be a unique minimum, and the optimal value.

steps.why: The gradient of ½xᵀHx is Hx when H is symmetric, and the gradient of bᵀx is b.
A stationary point has zero gradient; an invertible H gives a single solution.
Substitute x* = −H⁻¹b: ½bᵀH⁻¹b − bᵀH⁻¹b + c.
Expand using b = −Hx*; the result is an exact quadratic about x*.

steps.s: H ≻ 0 ⇒ f(x) > f(x*) for all x ≠ x*
steps.why: A positive definite quadratic form is positive for every nonzero argument.

derivs.result: x* = −H⁻¹b, unique minimum iff H ≻ 0, f* = c − ½bᵀH⁻¹b
checks: Scalar case f = ½hx² + bx gives x* = −b/h and f* = −b²/(2h), matching the formula.
An indefinite H gives a saddle point at x*.

derivs.title: Exact step along a direction
derivs.setup: For f(x) = ½xᵀAx − bᵀx with A ≻ 0, a point x with gradient g and a descent direction p (gᵀp < 0), derive the exact line search step α* and show it meets the Armijo condition for c₁ ≤ ½.

steps.s: φ(α) = f(x + αp) = f(x) + α gᵀp + ½α² pᵀAp
steps.why: Taylor expansion of a quadratic is exact, with gradient g and Hessian A.
Differentiate the one dimensional quadratic in α.
Set φ′(α) = 0; pᵀAp > 0 because A ≻ 0, so α* > 0 for a descent direction.
Substitute α* into φ: α*gᵀp + ½α*² pᵀAp = α*gᵀp − ½α*gᵀp.

steps.s: ½ α* gᵀp ≤ c₁ α* gᵀp for c₁ ≤ ½
steps.why: α*gᵀp < 0, so the inequality holds whenever c₁ is at most one half.

derivs.result: α* = −gᵀp/(pᵀAp); steepest descent p = −g gives α* = gᵀg/(gᵀAg)
checks: Steepest descent with A = I gives α* = 1, the exact jump to the minimizer.
This is why line searches use c₁ well below ½, typically 10⁻⁴.

derivs.title: Newton step from a quadratic model
derivs.setup: At iterate x_k with gradient g and Hessian H, derive the Newton step from the local quadratic model and the condition under which it is a descent direction.

steps.why: Second order Taylor model of f about x_k.
Differentiate the model with respect to the step p.
Set the model gradient to zero and solve the linear system Hp = −g.
Directional derivative of f along p_N at x_k.
H⁻¹ is positive definite when H is, so the quadratic form gᵀH⁻¹g is positive for g ≠ 0.

derivs.result: p_N = −H⁻¹g, a descent direction whenever H is positive definite
checks: On a strictly convex quadratic, one full Newton step lands exactly on the minimizer.
Near a minimizer with H ≻ 0 and Lipschitz Hessian, convergence is quadratic.

derivs.title: Cauchy point of a trust region
derivs.setup: Model m(p) = f + gᵀp + ½pᵀBp with trust region ‖p‖ ≤ Δ. Restricting p to the steepest descent direction, p = −τΔ g/‖g‖ with 0 ≤ τ ≤ 1, derive τ.

steps.why: Substitute p = −τΔ g/‖g‖ into the quadratic model.
Differentiate the one dimensional model in τ.
With zero or negative curvature m decreases monotonically, so the step goes to the boundary.
Positive curvature gives a convex parabola with an interior stationary point.
The interior minimizer is capped at the trust region boundary τ = 1.

derivs.result: p_C = −τΔ g/‖g‖ with τ = 1 if gᵀBg ≤ 0, else τ = min(1, ‖g‖³/(Δ gᵀBg))
checks: τ = 1 lands the step on the trust region boundary, ‖p‖ = Δ.
Interior case gives p = −(gᵀg/gᵀBg) g, the exact steepest descent step on the model.

derivs.title: KKT on a worked problem
derivs.setup: Minimize f = (x₁ − 2)² + (x₂ − 2)² subject to g = x₁ + x₂ − 2 ≤ 0. Use L = f + μg with μ ≥ 0 and find x*, μ*.

steps.why: Lagrangian with the inequality written as g ≤ 0 and multiplier μ.
Stationarity: ∇ₓL = 0.
Solve each stationarity equation for x in terms of μ.

steps.s: μ = 0 gives (2, 2) with g = 2 > 0, so g is active
steps.why: The unconstrained minimizer is infeasible, so complementary slackness requires g = 0.
Impose the active constraint x₁ + x₂ = 2.
Dual feasibility holds, so all KKT conditions are satisfied.

checks: −∇f(x*) = (2, 2) equals μ*∇g = 2·(1, 1): the objective gradient is balanced by the constraint gradient.
f is convex and g is linear, so the KKT point is the global minimum.

derivs.title: Multiplier as a sensitivity
derivs.setup: For min (x₁ − 2)² + (x₂ − 2)² subject to x₁ + x₂ ≤ b, show that the KKT multiplier equals −df*/db at b = 2.

steps.s: For b < 4 the constraint is active: x₁ + x₂ = b
steps.why: The unconstrained minimizer (2, 2) has sum 4, which exceeds b.
Symmetry of f about x₁ = x₂ places the optimum at the midpoint of the active line.
Substitute the optimum into the objective.
Differentiate the optimal value with respect to the constraint bound.
Envelope theorem: dL/db = −μ, so the multiplier is the shadow price of the bound.

checks: Relaxing the constraint (larger b) lowers f*, consistent with μ* ≥ 0.
At b = 4 the constraint becomes inactive and the formula gives μ* = 0.

derivs.title: Quadratic penalty and multiplier estimate
derivs.setup: Minimize f = x² subject to c(x) = x − 1 = 0 with the quadratic penalty Q(x; μ) = x² + (μ/2)(x − 1)². Convention L = f − λc, so λ* = 2. Derive x(μ) and the multiplier estimate.

steps.why: Minimize the smooth unconstrained penalty function.
Solve the linear stationarity equation for x.
Constraint violation shrinks like 1/μ.
Comparing ∇Q = 0 with ∇L = 0 gives the estimate λ ≈ −μc.
Both the iterate and the estimate converge to the constrained solution.

checks: Feasibility requires μ → ∞, which drives the Hessian 2 + μ toward ill conditioning.
Augmented Lagrangian adds a λ term so x reaches 1 at finite μ.

derivs.title: Least squares normal equations
derivs.setup: Fit ŷ = Xβ to data y (n points, p basis functions, X full column rank) by minimizing the sum of squared residuals. Derive the normal equations.

steps.why: Sum of squared residuals written in matrix form.
Expand the product; yᵀXβ is a scalar equal to βᵀXᵀy.
Differentiate the linear and quadratic terms in β.
Set the gradient to zero: the normal equations.
Full column rank makes XᵀX positive definite.

checks: Xᵀ(y − Xβ) = 0: residuals are orthogonal to every column of X.
Dimensions: XᵀX is p×p and Xᵀy is p×1.

derivs.title: Line fit by normal equations
derivs.setup: Fit ŷ = β₀ + β₁x to the points (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 4) by least squares.

steps.why: One row per point, columns for the constant and linear basis.
Entries are n, Σx, Σx, Σx².
Entries are Σy and Σxy.
Subtracting the first equation leaves 2β₁ = 3.
Back substitute into the first equation.

checks: Residuals (1/6, −1/3, 1/6) sum to zero, as required with a constant term.
Σxᵢrᵢ = 0 − 1/3 + 1/3 = 0, so residuals are orthogonal to the x column.

derivs.title: First order condition for convexity
derivs.setup: Let f be convex and differentiable. Derive f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀ(y − x) and conclude that any stationary point is a global minimizer.

steps.why: Definition of convexity along the segment from x to y.

steps.s: [f(x + t(y − x)) − f(x)] / t ≤ f(y) − f(x)
steps.why: Subtract f(x) and divide by t > 0.
Take t → 0⁺: the left side becomes the directional derivative.
Set x = x* in the inequality; the linear term vanishes.

derivs.result: f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀ(y − x); every stationary point of a convex f is a global minimum
checks: Geometrically, every tangent plane of a convex function is a global under estimator.
f = x² gives y² ≥ x² + 2x(y − x), equivalent to (y − x)² ≥ 0.

derivs.title: Weighted sum Pareto front
derivs.setup: Two objectives f₁ = x² and f₂ = (x − 2)². Use the weighted sum F = w f₁ + (1 − w) f₂ with w ∈ [0, 1] to trace the Pareto front.

steps.why: Scalarize the two objectives with a convex combination.
Stationarity of the scalarized objective.
Solve the linear equation; F″ = 2 > 0 confirms a minimum.
Evaluate each objective at x*(w).
Eliminate w: 2(1 − w) + 2w = 2.

checks: w = 1 gives x = 0, the minimizer of f₁; w = 0 gives x = 2, the minimizer of f₂.
The front is convex, so the weighted sum reaches every Pareto point.

derivs.title: Quadratic response surface size
derivs.setup: For n design variables, derive the number of coefficients in a full quadratic response surface and compare with the runs in a central composite design.

steps.s: ŷ = β₀ + Σβᵢxᵢ + Σβᵢᵢxᵢ² + Σ(i<j) βᵢⱼxᵢxⱼ
steps.why: Full second order model: constant, linear, pure quadratic and interaction terms.

steps.s: Constant, linear and pure quadratic terms: 1 + n + n = 1 + 2n
steps.why: One intercept, then one linear and one squared term per variable.
One cross term per unordered pair i < j.
Collect over a common denominator and factor.

steps.s: Fitting needs at least p distinct runs with XᵀX invertible
steps.why: Least squares has p unknowns and requires full column rank.
Factorial corners, axial star points and a center point support every term.

checks: n = 2: p = 6 and CCD = 9.
n = 3: p = 10 and CCD = 15.

derivs.title: Mattingly master equation
derivs.setup: Starting from an energy balance on the aircraft, derive the master equation for T_SL/W_TO in terms of W_TO/S, with T = αT_SL, W = βW_TO, load factor n and drag polar C_D = K₁C_L² + K₂C_L + C_D0.

steps.why: Excess power of thrust over drag R plus D changes the mechanical energy of the aircraft.
Lift equals n times weight.

steps.s: D + R = qS[K₁C_L² + K₂C_L + C_D0 + C_DR]
steps.why: Apply the drag polar plus additional drag coefficient C_DR.
Solve the energy balance for thrust and substitute T and W.
Normalizes thrust and wing loading by takeoff weight.

checks: Each term inside the braces is dimensionless, matching T/W.
Steady level flight (n = 1, P_s = 0, K₂ = 0) reduces to T/W = D/W.

derivs.title: Turn constraint bucket
derivs.setup: For the sustained level turn constraint T_SL/W_TO = (β/α)[qC_D0/(βW_TO/S) + K n² β(W_TO/S)/q], derive the wing loading at the minimum and the minimum T/W.

steps.why: Sustained turn has P_s = 0, K₂ = 0 and C_DR = 0 in the master equation.
The parasite term falls with w and the induced term rises, so a minimum exists.
Solve the stationarity condition.
Substitute w*: both terms equal n√(KC_D0).
The bucket is flight at the maximum L/D lift coefficient.

checks: Higher n moves the bucket to lower W/S and raises its floor in proportion to n.
At the bucket, parasite and induced drag are equal.

derivs.title: Breguet range (jet)
derivs.setup: Derive the range of a jet in steady level cruise with constant V, L/D and thrust specific fuel consumption c_t (weight of fuel per unit time per unit thrust).

steps.why: Steady level flight: thrust balances drag and lift balances weight.
Fuel burn rate is proportional to thrust.
Invert to get elapsed time per unit weight change.
Range accumulates at the flight speed.
Integrate from W_i to W_f with V, L/D and c_t held constant.

checks: Units: (m/s)/(1/s) = m.
Range grows with the product V·L/D, so jets cruise at the speed maximizing √C_L/C_D.

derivs.title: Breguet range (propeller)
derivs.setup: Derive the range of a propeller aircraft with propulsive efficiency η_p and power specific fuel consumption c_p (weight of fuel per unit time per unit shaft power), constant L/D.

steps.why: Steady level cruise: T = D and L = W.
Thrust power TV equals η_p times shaft power.
Fuel burn is proportional to shaft power.
Eliminate dt; the speed V cancels.
Integrate with η_p, c_p and L/D constant.

derivs.result: R = (η_p/c_p)(L/D) ln(W_i/W_f), maximized at (L/D)max where C_L = √(C_D0/K)
checks: c_p has units of 1/length here, so R has units of length.
Speed drops out, so the propeller optimum is at maximum L/D itself.

derivs.title: Gust load factor
derivs.setup: An aircraft in level flight at speed V with wing loading W/S and lift curve slope a meets a sharp edged vertical gust of speed U. Derive the incremental load factor.

steps.why: The vertical gust adds a small angle of attack U/V to the relative wind.
Lift increment from the lift curve slope.
Load factor increment is lift increment over weight.
Equivalent airspeeds with sea level density and gust alleviation factor K_g give the design form.

derivs.result: Δn = K_g ρ₀ U_e V_e a / (2 W/S)
checks: Δn is dimensionless: (kg/m³)(m/s)(m/s)/(N/m²).
Higher wing loading and lower lift slope reduce gust response; gust lines grow linearly with V.

derivs.title: Brayton cycle thermal efficiency
derivs.setup: Ideal Brayton cycle: isentropic compression 1→2, constant pressure heat addition 2→3, isentropic expansion 3→4, constant pressure heat rejection 4→1. Derive η_th in terms of compressor pressure ratio π_c.

steps.s: q_in = c_p(T₃ − T₂), q_out = c_p(T₄ − T₁)
steps.why: Constant pressure heat transfer for a calorically perfect gas; isentropic legs carry zero heat.
Net work over heat in, with w_net = q_in − q_out.
Both isentropic legs span the same pressure ratio.
Factor T₁ and T₂ out of the numerator and denominator.
Substitute the isentropic relation.

checks: π_c = 1 gives η_th = 0; η_th rises monotonically with π_c.
π_c = 30, γ = 1.4 gives η_th ≈ 0.62.

derivs.title: Propulsive efficiency
derivs.setup: A propulsor takes in air at flight speed V₀ and exhausts it at V_e with mass flow ṁ (fuel mass neglected, pressure matched exit). Derive the propulsive efficiency.

steps.why: Momentum balance on the stream tube.
Useful thrust power over the kinetic energy rate added to the stream.
Substitute the momentum thrust.
Factor V_e² − V₀² = (V_e − V₀)(V_e + V₀) and cancel.
Divide numerator and denominator by V₀.

checks: V_e → V₀ gives η_p → 1 with thrust → 0, which motivates high bypass engines moving more mass slowly.
η_p is dimensionless and lies in (0, 1] for V_e ≥ V₀.

derivs.title: Elliptic lift induced drag
derivs.setup: Using Prandtl lifting line, take the elliptic circulation Γ(y) = Γ₀√(1 − (2y/b)²) on a wing of span b, area S, AR = b²/S. Derive C_Di.

steps.why: Kutta-Joukowski integrated over the span; the ellipse area is πbΓ₀/4.
Divide L by ½ρV²S and invert.
The elliptic trailing vortex sheet induces a uniform downwash Γ₀/(2b).
Induced angle is downwash over freestream, with AR = b²/S.
Local lift tilts back by α_i, giving a drag component C_L α_i.

derivs.result: C_Di = C_L²/(π AR), e = 1 for the elliptic loading
checks: Induced drag vanishes as AR → ∞, recovering 2D airfoil behavior.
Any other loading gives C_Di = C_L²/(πeAR) with e < 1.

derivs.title: Hover momentum theory
derivs.setup: An actuator disk of area A in hover produces thrust T in air of density ρ. Derive the induced velocity v_h and ideal power.

steps.why: Momentum: air starts at rest far upstream and leaves at w far downstream.

steps.s: T v_i = ½ ṁ w² ⇒ w = 2v_i
steps.why: Power delivered at the disk equals kinetic energy flux added to the wake.
Mass flow through the disk at the induced velocity, with w = 2v_i.
Solve the thrust relation for the hover induced velocity.
Ideal induced power is thrust times induced velocity.

checks: Units: √(N/(kg/m³·m²)) = m/s.
Power per thrust P/T = √(DL/(2ρ)) grows with disk loading DL = T/A.

derivs.title: Axial climb induced velocity
derivs.setup: A rotor in axial climb at V_c carries the same thrust as in hover (hover induced velocity v_h). Using momentum theory, derive the induced velocity v_i and power.

steps.why: Mass flow through the disk includes the climb speed.
Energy balance again gives a far wake increment of 2v_i.

steps.s: T = 2ρA v_h² ⇒ v_i² + V_c v_i − v_h² = 0
steps.why: Equate with the hover thrust expression.
Take the positive root of the quadratic.
Power is thrust times the flow velocity through the disk.

checks: V_c = 0 recovers v_i = v_h.
Large V_c gives v_i → v_h²/V_c, so induced power falls toward T v_h²/V_c.

derivs.title: Torsional divergence of a typical section
derivs.setup: Rigid airfoil on a torsion spring k_θ at the elastic axis, lift acting at the aerodynamic center a distance e ahead of the elastic axis. Rigid incidence α₀, elastic twist θ. Derive θ and the divergence dynamic pressure.

steps.why: Lift depends on the total angle of attack including twist.

steps.s: k_θ θ = L e = qSeC_Lα(α₀ + θ)
steps.why: Moment balance about the elastic axis.
Collect the twist terms.
Solve for the elastic twist.
Twist grows without bound as the denominator reaches zero.

derivs.result: θ = (q/q_D)α₀/(1 − q/q_D), q_D = k_θ/(S e C_Lα)
checks: Units: (N·m/rad)/(m²·m) = N/m², a pressure.
Moving the elastic axis forward toward the AC (e → 0) raises q_D.

derivs.title: Point mass equations of motion
derivs.setup: Aircraft as a point mass in the vertical plane: flight path angle γ, thrust aligned with velocity, lift L normal to V, drag D, weight W = mg. Derive the equations of motion.

steps.s: v = V(cos γ, sin γ) ⇒ ẋ = V cos γ, ḣ = V sin γ
steps.why: Velocity of magnitude V along the flight path angle γ.
Differentiate v = V e_V; the unit vector e_V rotates at rate γ̇.

steps.s: Forces: (T − D − W sin γ) e_V + (L − W cos γ) e_n
steps.why: Resolve weight into path axes; T and D lie along e_V, L along e_n.

steps.s: mV̇ = T − D − W sin γ, mVγ̇ = L − W cos γ
steps.why: Project F = ma on e_V and e_n.
Steady level flight as the special case.

derivs.result: m V̇ = T − D − W sin γ, mVγ̇ = L − W cos γ, ḣ = V sin γ, ẋ = V cos γ
checks: Each force equation has units of newtons.
Steady climb (V̇ = 0, γ̇ = 0) gives sin γ = (T − D)/W.

derivs.title: Specific excess power
derivs.setup: From the tangential equation of motion m dV/dt = T − D − W sin γ, derive specific excess power and relate it to energy height.

steps.s: (T − D)V = W V sin γ + mV dV/dt
steps.why: Multiply the tangential equation by V and rearrange.
Kinematic relation for climb rate.
Divide by W = mg.
Energy height is mechanical energy per unit weight.
Differentiate h_e in time and compare with the P_s expression.

derivs.result: P_s = (T − D)V/W = dh_e/dt, h_e = h + V²/(2g)
checks: P_s has units of m/s, a rate of climb.
Constant speed gives P_s = dh/dt, the rate of climb.

derivs.title: Maximum L/D from the parabolic polar
derivs.setup: Given C_D = C_D0 + KC_L² with K = 1/(πeAR), derive the lift coefficient for maximum L/D and the value of (L/D)max.

steps.why: Ratio of lift to drag coefficients.
Quotient rule.
Solve the numerator for C_L.
At the optimum induced drag equals parasite drag.
Substitute C_D = 2C_D0.

checks: Doubling AR raises (L/D)max by √2.
Typical C_D0 = 0.02, K = 0.04 give (L/D)max ≈ 17.7.

derivs.title: Neutral point and static margin
derivs.setup: Wing body plus tail. Moments about the cg, h = x_cg/c̄, tail volume V_H = l_t S_t/(c̄S), tail efficiency η, downwash gradient dε/dα, total lift slope approximated by the wing body slope a. Derive h_n and SM.

steps.why: Tail angle of attack is reduced by downwash.

steps.s: C_m,cg = C_m,ac + aα(h − h_ac) − ηV_H a_t α_t
steps.why: Wing body lift acts at h_ac; tail lift a_t α_t acts aft at l_t.

steps.s: C_mα = a(h − h_ac) − ηV_H a_t(1 − dε/dα)
steps.why: Differentiate C_m,cg with respect to α.
Neutral point is the cg location where C_mα = 0.
Rewrite C_mα using h_n.

derivs.result: h_n = h_ac + ηV_H(a_t/a)(1 − dε/dα), SM = h_n − h = −C_mα/a
checks: Static stability requires C_mα < 0, so SM > 0 with the cg ahead of h_n.
A larger tail volume moves the neutral point aft.

derivs.title: Small strain from the deformation gradient
derivs.setup: With x = X + u(X) and F = ∂x/∂X, derive the Green-Lagrange strain and its small strain limit.

steps.why: Differentiate x = X + u with respect to X.
Squared length change of a material fiber, with dx = F dX.
Define E so that ds² − dS² = 2dXᵀE dX.
Substitute F = I + H into E.
Drop the quadratic term for small displacement gradients.
The skew part of H is the infinitesimal rotation, carrying zero strain.

checks: Rigid translation u = const gives E = 0.
Exact rigid rotation F = R gives E = 0, while ε is nonzero for finite rotation angles.

derivs.title: Cauchy tetrahedron
derivs.setup: A small tetrahedron has three faces normal to the coordinate axes and an oblique face of area dA with unit normal n. Derive the traction on the oblique face in terms of the stress tensor.

steps.why: Each coordinate face is the projection of the oblique face.

steps.s: t dA − Σ tᵢ dAᵢ + ρb dV = ρa dV
steps.why: Force balance; the face with outward normal −eᵢ carries traction −tᵢ.

steps.s: dV = h dA/3 → 0 faster than dA
steps.why: Shrink the height h; volume terms are of higher order.
Divide by dA and take h → 0.
Define σᵢⱼ as component j of the traction on the face normal to eᵢ.
Angular momentum balance gives σᵢⱼ = σⱼᵢ.

derivs.result: t(n) = σ n: traction is linear in the normal
checks: n = e₁ recovers t = t₁, the traction on the x₁ face.
Each term has units of force per area.

derivs.title: Bulk modulus from Lamé constants
derivs.setup: Isotropic linear elasticity σ = λ tr(ε) I + 2μ ε. Derive the bulk modulus K = −p/tr(ε) for hydrostatic stress σ = −pI, then express it in E and ν.

steps.why: Take the trace of the constitutive law; tr I = 3.
Hydrostatic stress has trace −3p.
Divide through by −3 tr ε.
Substitute λ = Eν/((1 + ν)(1 − 2ν)) and μ = E/(2(1 + ν)).
Combine over the common denominator 3(1 + ν)(1 − 2ν).

checks: ν → ½ gives K → ∞, the incompressible limit.
Steel, E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3 gives K ≈ 167 GPa.

derivs.title: Airy biharmonic from compatibility
derivs.setup: Plane stress, zero body force. Define σxx = φ,yy, σyy = φ,xx, σxy = −φ,xy. Use compatibility with tensor shear strain εxy to derive the equation for φ.

steps.why: Plane compatibility of a single valued displacement field.

steps.s: Eεxx = φ,yy − νφ,xx, Eεyy = φ,xx − νφ,yy, Eεxy = −(1 + ν)φ,xy
steps.why: Plane stress Hooke's law with G = E/(2(1 + ν)) and tensor shear strain.
Substitute the strains into compatibility and multiply by E.
The ν terms cancel.

checks: Equilibrium holds identically: σxx,x + σxy,y = φ,yyx − φ,xyy = 0.
The result is independent of elastic constants, so stresses in simply connected bodies with traction BCs are material independent.
Any polynomial φ of degree three or lower satisfies ∇⁴φ = 0 automatically.

derivs.title: Pure bending by an Airy function
derivs.setup: Beam strip −c ≤ y ≤ c, unit thickness, end moment M with convention M = ∫σxx y dy. Take φ = Cy³ and find C and the stress.

steps.why: Any cubic satisfies the biharmonic equation.
Apply the Airy definitions.

steps.s: Top and bottom faces traction free; ∫σxx dy = 0
steps.why: σyy and σxy vanish everywhere, and σxx is odd in y, so the end carries zero net force.
Moment resultant at the end equals M.
Solve for C and substitute.

checks: The elasticity solution matches elementary beam theory exactly for pure bending.
Stress is linear in y with zero on the centroidal axis.

derivs.title: Thin cylinder hoop and axial stress
derivs.setup: Closed thin cylinder of radius r, wall thickness t ≪ r, internal pressure p. Derive the axial stress, then the hoop stress, and compare them.

steps.s: Cross section cut: p πr² = σx 2πr t
steps.why: End cap pressure force is carried by the wall ring of area 2πrt.
Solve the axial balance.

steps.s: Diametral cut over length L: 2σθ t L = p·2rL
steps.why: Pressure on the projected area 2rL is carried by two wall cuts.
Solve the hoop balance.
Compare the two results.

checks: Radial stress is of order p, small compared with pr/t since r/t ≫ 1.
Units: Pa·m/m = Pa.

derivs.title: Lamé thick cylinder
derivs.setup: Thick cylinder, inner radius a, outer radius b, pressures p_i inside and p_o outside, axisymmetric and in plane strain or plane stress. Derive σr and σθ.

steps.why: Radial equilibrium of an annular element.
Axisymmetric kinematics.
Hooke's law in equilibrium gives d/dr[(1/r)d(ru)/dr] = 0.

steps.s: σr = A − B/r², σθ = A + B/r²
steps.why: Stresses from the displacement solution.
Pressure boundary conditions, compressive radial stress.

steps.s: A = (p_i a² − p_o b²)/(b² − a²), B = (p_i − p_o)a²b²/(b² − a²)
steps.why: Solve the two linear equations.

derivs.result: σr,θ = (p_i a² − p_o b²)/(b² − a²) ∓ (p_i − p_o)a²b²/((b² − a²)r²)
checks: σr + σθ = 2A is constant through the wall.
b = a + t with t → 0 and p_o = 0 gives σθ(a) → p_i a/t, the thin wall result.

derivs.title: Flexure formula
derivs.setup: Euler-Bernoulli beam, y measured up from the neutral axis, positive M sagging, curvature κ. Derive the bending stress.

steps.why: Plane sections remain plane and normal to the deformed axis.
Uniaxial Hooke's law in the fibers.
Pure bending has zero axial force, placing the neutral axis at the centroid.
Moment resultant of the fiber stresses.
Eliminate κ = M/(EI).

checks: Positive M puts the top fibers (y > 0) in compression.
Units: N·m·m/m⁴ = Pa.

derivs.title: Bredt-Batho shear flow
derivs.setup: Single cell closed thin walled section under torque T, enclosed area A, wall thickness t(s). Derive the shear flow and shear stress.

steps.why: Axial equilibrium of a wall element under pure torsion.
Torque from shear flow with moment arm r_n about any point.
Each wall element and the pole form a triangle of area ½ r_n ds.
∮ r_n ds = 2A for the closed contour.
Shear stress is shear flow over local thickness.

checks: Maximum stress sits at the thinnest wall.
Units: N·m/m² = N/m, a force per length.

derivs.title: Twist rate of a closed cell
derivs.setup: For the same single cell section with q = T/(2A), shear modulus G, derive the twist rate dθ/dz and the torsion constant J.

steps.why: Hooke's law in shear for the wall.
Strain energy per unit length: ½τγ t integrated around the wall.
External work per unit length of a linear torque on the twist rate.
Equate energies and substitute q = T/(2A).
Write dθ/dz = T/(GJ).

checks: Thin circular tube: A = πr², ∮ds/t = 2πr/t gives J = 2πr³t, matching the polar moment.
Units of J: m⁴.

derivs.title: Rayleigh-Ritz cantilever
derivs.setup: Cantilever of length L, stiffness EI, tip load P, clamped at x = 0. Use w = a x² (satisfying w(0) = w′(0) = 0) and minimize total potential energy.

steps.why: Strain energy of bending minus potential of the load.
Integrate the constant curvature over the length.
Substitute w(L) = aL².
Stationary potential energy.
Evaluate the tip deflection.

checks: Ritz approximations are too stiff, so the deflection is smaller than exact.
A cubic trial term recovers the exact PL³/(3EI).

derivs.title: Rigid bar with rotational spring
derivs.setup: Rigid bar of length L pinned at its base with rotational spring k, vertical load P at the top, rotation θ. Find the critical load and the post-buckling path.

steps.why: Spring energy minus load potential; the load drops by L(1 − cos θ).
Equilibrium is stationary potential energy.

steps.s: θ = 0, or P = kθ/(L sin θ)
steps.why: Trivial path and the bifurcated branch.

steps.s: d²Π/dθ² = k − PL cos θ; at θ = 0, zero at P = k/L
steps.why: Loss of positive definiteness on the trivial path.
The branch carries increasing load after bifurcation.

checks: Units: (N·m/rad)/m = N.
θ/sin θ ≈ 1 + θ²/6 for small θ, a rising parabola.

derivs.title: Two DOF bifurcation
derivs.setup: Two rigid links of length L stacked vertically: rotational spring k at the base and k at the middle hinge, vertical load P at the top. Absolute link rotations θ₁, θ₂. Find P_cr and the mode.

steps.why: The middle spring sees the relative rotation.
Load potential −PL Σ(1 − cos θ) with 1 − cos θ ≈ θ²/2 for each link.
Hessian of Π = U + V about the straight state.
Critical loads make the stability matrix singular.
Smallest root of the quadratic in PL/k.
Mode shape from the first row of Kθ = 0.

checks: The second root (3 + √5)k/(2L) ≈ 2.62k/L has θ₂/θ₁ < 0, an S shaped mode.
Both links rotate the same way in the first mode, as in a cantilever column.

derivs.title: Propped cantilever by superposition
derivs.setup: Beam fixed at x = 0, simply supported at x = L, uniform load w, stiffness EI. Find the prop reaction R and the fixed end moment.

steps.s: Release the prop: δ_w = wL⁴/(8EI) down, δ_R = RL³/(3EI) up
steps.why: Determinate cantilever under the load and under the redundant R separately.
Compatibility: zero deflection at the prop.
Solve the compatibility equation.
Moment equilibrium about the fixed end.

derivs.result: R = 3wL/8, fixed end reaction 5wL/8, M₀ = wL²/8 (hogging)
checks: Vertical reactions sum to wL.
Fixed end moment equals the simply supported midspan moment wL²/8.

derivs.title: Quarter ring by Castigliano
derivs.setup: Quarter circle bar of radius R, center O. Free end A on the horizontal radius, fixed end B on the vertical radius, vertical load P at A. Bending energy only; find the vertical deflection at A.

steps.why: θ measured from OA; the horizontal arm from A to the section is R(1 − cos θ).

steps.s: U = ∫ M²/(2EI) R dθ, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2
steps.why: Bending energy with ds = R dθ.
Castigliano's second theorem.

steps.s: ∫(0 to π/2)(1 − 2cos θ + cos²θ)dθ = π/2 − 2 + π/4
steps.why: Integrate term by term.
Combine the terms.

checks: Units: N·m³/(N·m²) = m.
Thin ring assumption R ≫ depth justifies the straight beam bending energy.

derivs.title: Neo-Hookean uniaxial tension
derivs.setup: Incompressible neo-Hookean solid, W = (μ/2)(λ₁² + λ₂² + λ₃² − 3), stretched uniaxially with stretch λ and free lateral faces. Derive the nominal and Cauchy stress.

steps.why: Incompressibility λ₁λ₂λ₃ = 1 with lateral symmetry.
Substitute the principal stretches.
Nominal (first Piola) stress is work conjugate to λ.
Cauchy stress uses the deformed area, smaller by 1/λ.
Linearize about the reference state.

derivs.result: P = μ(λ − λ⁻²), σ = μ(λ² − λ⁻¹), small strain E = 3μ
checks: λ = 1 gives zero stress.
E = 3μ matches E = 2μ(1 + ν) with ν = ½.

derivs.title: Continuity equation
derivs.setup: Derive the local Eulerian form of mass conservation from conservation of mass of a material volume, using J = det F.

steps.s: ∫ρ₀ dV₀ = ∫ρ dV for every material volume
steps.why: Mass of a material body is constant.
Volume change under the deformation gradient.
Arbitrary volume localizes the integral statement: Lagrangian form.
Material time derivative; Euler's formula for J̇.
Divide by J > 0.
Expand Dρ/Dt = ∂ρ/∂t + v·∇ρ.

checks: Incompressible motion: Dρ/Dt = 0 ⇒ ∇·v = 0.
Each term has units of kg/(m³·s).

derivs.title: Euler column
derivs.setup: Pinned-pinned column of length L, stiffness EI, axial compressive load P, lateral deflection w(x), with internal moment M = −Pw. Derive the critical load.

steps.why: Moment-curvature relation with M = −Pw from the deflected free body.
Rearrange into a constant coefficient ODE.

steps.s: w = A sin kx + B cos kx
steps.why: General solution.
Pin at the base.

steps.s: w(L) = 0 ⇒ A sin kL = 0 with A ≠ 0 ⇒ kL = nπ
steps.why: Nontrivial equilibrium in the bent shape.
Smallest load, n = 1.

derivs.result: P_cr = π²EI/L², mode w = A sin(πx/L)
checks: Units: N·m²/m² = N.
Other end conditions give P_cr = π²EI/(KL)² with effective length factor K.

derivs.title: Imperfect column and Southwell plot
derivs.setup: Pinned-pinned column with initial crookedness w₀ = a₀ sin(πx/L), total deflection w, load P, P_cr = π²EI/L². Derive the amplification and the Southwell relation.

steps.why: Bending moment produces only the change in curvature from the initial shape.
Trial shape matching the imperfection mode.
Substitute and cancel sin(πx/L).
Solve for the total amplitude.
Measured additional deflection.
Rearrange: δ/P against δ is a line of slope 1/P_cr.

derivs.result: a = a₀/(1 − P/P_cr); Southwell: slope of δ/P vs δ is 1/P_cr
checks: P → P_cr gives a → ∞, approaching the perfect column bifurcation load asymptotically.
a₀ = 0 gives a = 0 for all P below P_cr.

derivs.title: Axial CTE of a unidirectional composite
derivs.setup: Fibers and matrix bonded in parallel along the fiber direction, moduli E_f, E_m, volume fractions V_f, V_m, CTEs α_f, α_m, uniform ΔT, zero applied load. Derive the composite axial CTE.

steps.why: Iso-strain: perfect bonding along the fiber axis.

steps.s: σ_f = E_f(ε − α_fΔT), σ_m = E_m(ε − α_mΔT)
steps.why: Thermoelastic Hooke's law in each phase.
Zero net axial force with no applied load.
Solve the force balance for ε.
Composite CTE is free strain per unit temperature change.

checks: α_f = α_m gives α₁ = α_f.
Stiff fibers (E_f ≫ E_m) pull α₁ toward α_f.
